entries.title: Germany news: Merz to speak at CSU party conference
entries.summary: With his coalition under pressure, Merz will speak at the close of the CSU party conference. Meanwhile, fire has largely destroyed Hitler's former Eagle's Nest retreat. DW has more
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Merz to speak at CSU party conference

Published October 24, 2026last updated October 24, 2026

With his coalition under pressure, Merz will speak at the close of the CSU party conference. Meanwhile, fire has largely destroyed Hitler's former Eagle's Nest retreat. DW has more

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Chancellor Friedrich Merz will speak at the close of the Bavarian CSU party conference
  • The 2-day conference comes as Merz's coalition of the CDU, CSU and SPD faces a high degree of dissatisfaction
  • A fire has largely destroyed the mountain retreat formerly used by Hitler, known as Eagle's Nest.

Read below for a roundup of stories making news in Germany for the weekend of October 24-25.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Merz set to address Bavarian conservatives as party conference wraps up

Merz set to address Bavarian conservatives as party conference wraps up

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is set to make an address at the Munich exhibition hall as the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) closes its two-day party conference.

Merz's speech comes at a turbulent time for the CDU/CSU alliance and expectations among delegates for the speech by the leader of the conservative bloc are mixed.

The CSU is the Bavarian sister party of Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and there remain a number of key issues that have many in the CSU concerned over the future of the party at a national level.

A point of contention is who from the conservative bloc will succeed outgoing President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, with there being no clarity as yet from Merz or CSU leader Markus Söder, as to who their candidate would be.

Coupled with that leadership question, there is discontent over the pace of implementation of reforms of Germany's retirement, nursing care and health insurance systems.

There is also concern over a strategy to deal with the rise of the far-right in the form of the Alternative for Germany party (AfD).

Skip next section Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat catches fire, police say

Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat catches fire, police say

A fire broke out on Friday evening at the Kehlsteinhaus in Bavaria more commonly known as the Eagle's Nest and used as a retreat by Adolf Hitler and Nazi officials.

The Kehlsteinhaus was engulfed in flames, a police statement read, adding that a suspect has been arrested and the incident was being criminally investigated.

Read more about that here. 

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Morgen from a chilly newsroom here in Bonn.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz is set to address his CDU's Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CSU) as their 2-day party conference wraps up in Munich.

The coalition government that Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the CSU belong to along with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) is facing a number of challenges.

There has been speculation over the political future of Merz's coalition, consiting of CDU, the CSU and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), folllowing a string of electoral setbacks and policy issues.

And then overnight, a fire has ripped through the one-time retreat in the Bavarian Alps, built for Nazi leader Adolf Hitler.

Stay tuned for the latest on these stories and more from Germany this weekend.

entries.title: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un arrives in Chinese border city
entries.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has reportedly arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong via a newly opened bridge linking the two countries, South Korea's Yonhap news agency said.
entries.content:
China

Kim Jong Un arrives in China via newly opened border bridge — reports

October 24, 2026

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has reportedly arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong via a newly opened bridge linking the two countries, South Korea's Yonhap news agency said.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un arrived in China via the newly opened bridge, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency reported on Saturday.

"It appears that Kim Jong Un has arrived in Dandong, China, via the New Yalu River Bridge," the unnamed source said.

The four-lane bridge was completed in 2014 but remained unused for 12 years due to a lack of connecting roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side.

It officially opened about a week ago, marking a step towards strengthening economic ties between the neighbouring countries.

China is North Korea’s largest trading partner and a key source of diplomatic, economic and political support for the isolated, nuclear-armed state, although relations between the two have not always been smooth.

Kim’s trip coincides with key dates in China

Neither Beijing nor Pyongyang has confirmed Kim’s visit.

The trip coincides with the anniversary of China’s entry into the Korean War, known in China as the "War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea." It remains unclear whether Kim will attend commemorative events.

During the 1950-53 war, Chinese troops fought alongside North Korea against South Korea and US-led United Nations forces.

Kim’s visit also comes ahead of a key political meeting in Beijing on Monday, when Chinese President Xi Jinping and other senior officials gather for the fifth plenary session of the Communist Party’s powerful Central Committee.

Bridge highlights North Korea's ties with China

The New Yalu River Bridge opened just over a month after North Korea and Russia inaugurated their first road bridge, which Pyongyang hailed as a sign of closer ties.

While North Korea’s trade with Russia largely involves military supplies, trade with China could provide goods needed to develop its civilian economy, analysts say.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: France protests: More violence feared amid renewed demonstrations
entries.summary: France is deploying some 70,000 police officers as fresh nationwide protests begin. A deadly shooting near Paris has additionally fueled tensions. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
France

France protests: Demonstrations resume with more violence feared

Published October 24, 2026last updated October 24, 2026

France is deploying some 70,000 police officers as fresh nationwide protests begin. A deadly shooting near Paris has additionally fueled tensions. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to take to France's streets to protest over the rising cost of living, declining social services and inequality
  • Authorities are looking to prevent a repeat of the violence that took place at similar protests a week ago with heightened security and bans
  • President Emmanuel Macron has called a shooting near Paris in which one person died and five were injured 'a racist terrorist attack'
  • Protests are also expected in eight Italian cities, including Rome and Milan

Follow below for the latest on the protests and unrest in France and other parts of Europe on Saturday, October 24, 2026:

Skip next section Teargas fired at small protest in Lyon — AFP journalist

Teargas fired at small protest in Lyon — AFP journalist

Police have used teargas grenades to disperse a small protest in an area banned to all demonstrations in the southeastern city of Lyon, according to a journalist from the French news agency Agence France-Presse (AFP).

The group was protesting near a university faculty and the city's police station, according to AFP.

The agency said the police took action as the protesters tried to block the road.

Skip next section IN PICTURES: Paris boutiques behind boards

IN PICTURES: Paris boutiques behind boards

Many store owners across France have taken their own precautionary measures to protect their premises against vandalism despite a high police presence meant to guarantee security.

Several glitzy facades of prestigious shops in the capital, Paris, have now disappeared behind boards.

Here are some pictures of the current face of one of the world's most famous shopping hubs.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Are French police the most violent in the EU?

IN DEPTH: Are French police the most violent in the EU?

With some 70,000 police officers to be deployed on Saturday, many people in France are fearing repeat violence not just from certain groups of protesters but also from the forces of law and order.

During recent student protests, a number of teenagers sustained serious injuries amid police actions, and multiple unconfirmed videos have shown incidents of brutality toward protesters at last week's wider demonstrations.

French police are among the most heavily armed in Europe and are subjected to less independent oversight than in many other countries.

Rights group Amnesty International has described the police response to the current protests as "disproportionate" and called upon French authorities to "act upon their human rights obligations." 

This DW article looks at the criticism leveled at French police and the differences between policing in France and elsewhere: Are the French police the most violent in the EU?

Skip next section Orleans protests expected to target Le Pen's party congress

Orleans protests expected to target Le Pen's party congress

A two-day congress of the far-right National Rally (RN) party in the city of Orleans, some 110 km (70 miles) south of Paris, is expected to draw its own protest by labor unions, left-wing parties, students and anti-racism groups.

The congress is to be hosted by Marine Le Pen, the party's lead candidate at French presidential elections in six months time.

Authorities fear clashes between counterprotesters and supporters of Le Pen, who has a nationalist, anti-immigration agenda and has received upwind from the recent protests by taking a strong law-and-order stance and citing "anarchic immigration" as one factor behind them.

The congress is likely to see the reelection of party president, Jordan Bardella.

Skip next section France puts high security in place for fresh protests

France puts high security in place for fresh protests

French authorities say they will be deploying some 70,000 police on Saturday amid renewed protests as they look to prevent a repeat of the violence that marred mass nationwide demonstrations over social inequality a week ago.

Announcing the deployment, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned at a news conference in Paris that calls for violence and looting were circulating on social media.

Several restrictions on protests have been imposed across the country, including bans on a union-led march on one route in the capital, Paris, that organizers say they will disregard, citing safety concerns about a proposed alternative.

Leading museums in Paris, including the Louvre, will also remained closed.

The protests come a critical political moment for France, with elections due in six months to elect a successor to President Emmanual Macron.

Polls have shown far-right candidate Marine Le Pen as the frontrunner and indicated that the latest events might have shored up her popularity.

You can read more about the security precautions and background to the protests in France in this article:France to deploy 70,000 police officers ahead of protests

Skip next section Macron calls shooting near Paris a 'racist terrorist attack'

Macron calls shooting near Paris a 'racist terrorist attack'

French President Emmanuel Macron has condemned a shooting near Paris on Friday in which one person was killed and five others were injured, including a 12-year-old girl.

Macron called the attack "a turning point," saying it was "a terrorist act that was planned ​to kill our compatriots, our children, based on the color of their skin or their religion."

The victim killed was said by authorities to have been of "African origin," and most of the injured were also from foreign backgrounds.

The shooting is likely to further fuel tensions ahead of protests planned for Saturday, with some far-right politicians blaming immigration for the violence on the sidelines of protests in several French cities on October 17.

You can read more about the attack in this article: France: 1 killed, 4 wounded after shooting near Paris

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

France is bracing for another day of mass protests a week after the country saw some violent rioting on the sidelines of demonstrations against rising inequality, declining public services and a deteriorating education system.

The current wave of protests sweeping the country comes on the heels of largely peaceful demonstrations by high school students over learning conditions.

Some 70,000 police are to be deployed in the capital, Paris, and other cities, while protest bans are in place in several locations.

The protests in France have spilled over into other European countries, with Italy also expecting mass demonstrations on Saturday.

In this blog, we will be keeping you up to date on all the latest protest developments in France and other European countries on Saturday, October 24, and Sunday, October 25.

entries.title: Taiwan: Typhoon Champi leaves 1 dead, over 500 injured
entries.summary: After killing one person and causing major disruptions in Taiwan, Typhoon Champi is now headed towards China.
entries.content:
Taiwan

Typhoon Champi leaves 1 dead, more than 500 injured in Taiwan

October 24, 2026

After killing one person and causing major disruptions in Taiwan, Typhoon Champi is now headed towards China.

Typhoon Champi killed at least one person and left more than 500 people with injuries as it passed through Taiwan on Saturday.

Taiwan's fire department said the death toll remained at 1, after a man was swept ​away by waves from the island of Liuqiu. At least 527 others were injured during the heavy wind and torrential rain.

Several parts in Taiwan received heavy rain and strong winds that prompted authorities to cut off power, leaving thousands of people without power supply.

Some 280,000 households were knocked out of power, according to United Daily News, a local Taiwanese newspaper. By Saturday morning, the power supply was restored to 80% of the households.

Champi also led to 259 flights cancellations, an improvement from Friday, ⁠when ​the number was almost 1,000, the Transport Ministry said.

Several trees were downed amid strong gusts In the capital Taipei.

Authorities in several districts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second day of office and school closures on Saturday.

Champi headed to China

The typhoon continued to weaken as it moved north towards the Chinese coast though it was not expected to make landfall there.

Chinese authorities have sent a team to ​the eastern province of Zhejiang as Champi ⁠approached, warning of strong winds and heavy rain through Sunday.

It said it had readied 400 rescue workers and 600 pieces of equipment, ⁠while more than 41,000 firefighters were on ​emergency duty.

Typhoon Champi started out as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the Pacific this year. While it is weakening, Champi is still packing ​gusts of around 78 km/h (126 mph) near its center, according to Taiwan's Central Weather Administration (CWA).

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: India news: India-China border tensions back in focus despite ongoing talks
entries.summary: India says Chinese forces deviating from established patrolling patterns continue to disrupt the border situation, a day after the ITBP chief reported face-offs at multiple locations in Arunachal Pradesh. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India news: China border tensions back in focus despite talks

Published October 24, 2026last updated October 24, 2026

India says Chinese forces deviating from established patrolling patterns continue to disrupt the border situation, a day after the ITBP chief reported face-offs at multiple locations in Arunachal Pradesh. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Indian Foreign Ministry blamed Chinese patrolling deviations for border disruptions
  • India said both sides are using diplomatic and military mechanisms to resolve outstanding issues
  • Three children among five killed in firecracker workshop explosions in Bihar
  • Jio Platforms IPO draws record demand, subscribed more than 22 times
  • Violence in Arunachal over proposed hydropower project

Here are the top headlines from India on Saturday, October 24:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Five killed in blast during roadwork in Andhra Pradesh

Five killed in blast during roadwork in Andhra Pradesh

Five people were killed on Saturday when explosive material misfired during road-widening work in the southern state of Andhra Pradesh, the Hindustan Times reported citing the police.

The blast occurred in Pinakota village in Alluri Sitharama Raju district during rock blasting for road expansion.

The explosion also destroyed two vehicles, the report said.

State Home Minister Vangalapudi Anitha expressed condolences to the victims' families and directed officials to ensure medical treatment for the injured and provide assistance to those affected.

Skip next section Violence in Arunachal over proposed hydropower project

Violence in Arunachal over proposed hydropower project

A police station was reportedly burnt down and seven police vehicles torched on Friday by angry protesters opposing a proposed hydropower project in Pasighat in the northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh, the Arunachal Times newspaper said.

The violence broke out in Pasighat after police fired tear gas at youths protesting the proposed 11,000-megawatt Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP), according to local media.

Protesters also allegedly set fire to a National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC) office, while a journalist was injured in the unrest, reports said.

Protesters are demanding the release of detained activists, the withdrawal of security forces from the Siang region and an immediate halt to survey work on the hydropower project.

Authorities have deployed additional security personnel in the region as tensions remained high.

Skip next section Jio Platforms IPO draws record demand, subscribed more than 22 times

Jio Platforms IPO draws record demand, subscribed more than 22 times

Bids for Jio Platforms' initial public offering (IPO) topped $77 billion (€68.74 billion) on Friday, making it India's most subscribed share offering. Demand exceeded 22 times the shares on offer.

The IPO of the telecoms and digital unit of Reliance Industries, owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani, attracted more than 13.8 million applications — a record for India.

The offering values Jio Platforms at up to $108.3 billion.

Led by Ambani's son Akash, the company operates a mobile network serving more than 500 million users and counts Meta and Google among its investors.

The shares are expected to list on Wednesday.

The IPO comes just days after Elon Musk criticized regulatory delays facing Starlink in India, accusing Reliance Industries head Mukesh Ambani of keeping Starlink out of the India market.

Skip next section Three children among five killed in firecracker workshop explosions in Bihar

Three children among five killed in firecracker workshop explosions in Bihar

Three children were among the five killed on Friday when a series of explosions ripped through a firecracker workshop operating from a private home in the eastern state of Bihar, police said.

According to the police residents fear more people may be buried under the rubble.

The workshop's owner and four relatives were among those killed in the incident in Siwan district.

According to the Hindustan Times newspaper, a witness said that body parts of some of those killed in the blast were "strewn all over."

Industrial accidents, especially in firework factories, are common in India, where safety standards are often poorly enforced.

In recent past:

  • In August, 11 people, including eight children, were killed by an explosion in a firecracker workshop operating from a residential area in northern Uttar Pradesh state
  • In March, a fire at a fireworks factory in Maharashtra state India killed 17 people and injured 18 people
  • In April, eight people were killed and 15 injured when a firecracker warehouse in Kerala in south India caught fire

Skip next section India blames Chinese patrolling deviations for border disruptions

India blames Chinese patrolling deviations for border disruptions

India's Foreign Ministry said on Friday the situation along the India-China border was periodically disrupted when Chinese forces deviated from established patrolling patterns.

"Both sides continue to use existing diplomatic and military mechanisms to resolve outstanding issues and avoid misunderstandings and miscalculations along the Line of Actual Control (LAC)," the ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said while addressing the media.

The two countries have also agreed to discuss ways to improve their understanding of the LAC in certain areas to strengthen border management, he added.

"I would also like to emphasize that maintaining peace and tranquillity in the border areas is essential for the overall development of bilateral relations," Jaiswal said.

'Face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops continuing'

This development comes a day after India's China border police chief, Shatrujeet Singh Kapur, said on Thursday that face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops are continuing at multiple locations along the border in the northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh, despite ongoing talks between the two countries, according to Indian media.

The face-offs in Arunachal Pradesh underscore the challenges of maintaining peace along the border even as the two countries have held several rounds of military and diplomatic talks this year.

The issue was also taken up by the opposition Congress party with Member of Parliament and senior party leader Jairam Ramesh criticizing Prime Minister Narendra Modi and and the government for "remain silent on this grave issue."

"The nation is asking: Amid ongoing tensions on the border, what kind of nationalism is this softness toward China and the growing economic dependence?" Ramesh posted on X.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage!

Welcome to our coverage!

Hello! This is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi Studio bringing you the top updates from across India.

The issue of India-China border tensions has its made its way back into focus as India on Friday said Chinese forces deviating from established patrolling patterns continue to disrupt the border situation.

Meanwhile, in the eastern state of Bihar, three children were among the five killed when a series of powerful explosions tore through a firecracker workshop at a private house, where the manufacturing was taking place.

For all this and more, follow our liveblog.

entries.title: Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat catches fire, police say
entries.summary: Authorities have arrested a suspect as firemen try to put out the fire in Bavaria, near the Austrian border.
entries.content:
Germany

Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat catches fire, police say

October 24, 2026

Authorities have arrested a suspect as firemen try to put out the fire in Bavaria, near the Austrian border.

A fire broke out on Friday evening at the Kehlsteinhaus in Bavaria, more commonly known as the Eagle's Nest and used as a retreat by Adolf Hitler and Nazi officials.

The Kehlsteinhaus was engulfed in flames, a police statement read, adding that a suspect has been arrested and the incident was being criminally investigated.

What do we know so far about the Kehlsteinhaus fire?

A fire alarm went off at the Kehlsteinhaus on the Obersalzberg in Berchtesgaden at around 9:15 p.m. local time (1915 GMT) on Friday, the police said in a statement.

"The fire brigades, who were alerted immediately, could already see flames clearly visible at the Kehlsteinhaus as they approached," the police statement read.

Some 200 firefighters and emergency personnel were deployed to the site. Firefighters struggled to reach the Kehlsteinhaus, which sits at some 1,834 meters (6,017 feet) above sea level, with their engines.

Police added that the building and its immediate vicinity could only be entered while wearing respiratory protective equipment (RPE).

Police said they were unaware of any injuries as of yet.

The site once housed Hitler's heavily fortified country residence, where he is believed to have partially written his book "Mein Kampf." It was built in 1938 as a guest house for Nazi officials.

It remains a symbol of the Nazi regime and is among only a few monuments of the Hitler era that survived the World War II bombing unscathed. Today, it is classified as a historical monument and is home to a popular restaurant.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: France to deploy 70,000 police officers ahead of protests
entries.summary: With new protests in France planned for this weekend, the authorities pledged to do everything in their power to prevent looting, violence and vandalism.
entries.content:
France

France to deploy 70,000 police officers ahead of protests

October 24, 2026

With new protests in France planned for this weekend, the authorities pledged to do everything in their power to prevent looting, violence and vandalism.

As France braces for new protests on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned that calls for violence and looting were circulating online and pledged to deploy 70,000 police officers to secure order across the country.

"We will be uncompromising with rioters, looters and all those who commit acts of violence," Nunez told reporters on Friday.

The regular police officers will be reinforced by elite units, mounted police and heavy vehicles, and also equipped with helicopters, water cannon, drones and anti-drone systems, according to the minister.

"We will be extremely vigilant," he added, vowing to "let absolutely nothing pass."

Paris storekeepers prepare for more looting

The apparent show of force comes a week after riots ripped through Paris and other major cities.

While the ongoing political standoff started with students demanding better facilities, more teachers, and other improvements to the country's education system, it has grown into a general outpouring of anger over the cost of living.

Last Saturday, the protests escalated into violent riots, with authorities accusing radical militants and bands of young looters of taking advantage of the protesters' anger to sow chaos.

Police have faced groups of masked looters burning cars and buildings. Thousands of stores were ransacked.

Addressing reporters on Friday, the interior minister said that the unrest was "completely unacceptable" and said the authorities "will do everything in our power" to avoid a repeat of the violence.

Meanwhile, Paris shopkeepers were seen boarding up their windows. The city council called on residents and business owners to remove objects that could be set on fire or used as either projectiles or barricades.

Who will be marching on Saturday?

Nunez also said authorities will maintain curfews in designated areas of the city. This will include restrictions between 11 pm and 6 am in two central Paris squares, according to the local police.

The police approved only one protest march, organized by labor union CGT, on a limited route through Paris on Saturday. The authorities rejected requests by France's biggest student union UNEF and its anti-establishment Yellow Vest movement to hold their own rallies.

However, UNEF pledged to go ahead with its protest regardless, while Yellow Vest supporters were expected to join the official march.

Authorities had banned all protests in France's second largest city, Marseille, before walking the decision back and allowing a union demonstration. Authorities also intend to keep protesters away from the center of Lyon, France's third most populous city.

Students 'not satisfied' after meeting Macron

The government, led by centrist President Emmanuel Macron, sought to differentiate between what they see as legitimate protests and the violent unrest.

Macron himself also dismissed the narrative that Islamist extremists and migrants were driving the violence. He has, however, pointed to far-left groups and accused them of trying to stage a coup.

On Friday, Macron also held his first-ever meeting with representatives of secondary school students. However, the meeting ended with the pupils calling for more protests.

"We are not satisfied," said student representative Nathanael Combary, president of campaign group High School Renewal.

He told reporters that the president had been "attentive" but that the students were still waiting for concrete proposals to be presented at their meeting with the prime minister on Monday.

He urged his fellow students to "continue to mobilize" and maintain a "standoff" with the government.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Ebola: Kenya announces second death
entries.summary: Kenyan health officials said the 65-year-old ​woman was a close ‌relative of a ‌​man who died of Ebola last month. The woman developed symptoms ‌while under quarantine in Nairobi.
entries.content:
October 23, 2026

Kenyan health officials said the 65-year-old ​woman was a close ‌relative of a ‌​man who died of Ebola last month. The woman developed symptoms ‌while under quarantine in Nairobi.

Kenya has recorded a second Ebola death, the Health Ministry said on Friday.

Officials identified the patient as a 65-year-old woman, a close relative of a Kenyan man who died of Ebola earlier this month.

The woman began showing symptoms 10 days ago while in quarantine. She began receiving supportive care at an infectious disease unit in the capital, Nairobi.

"Sadly, she succumbed to ⁠the ​disease early ​this evening," the ministry said.

Medical personnel "did everything possible to save her life," the ministry said, adding that it had notified her family and would arrange a safe and dignified burial in consultation with relatives.

Seven people continue to receive treatment for the illness in Kenya.

What else do we know about the 2nd Kenyan Ebola death?

Kenya's first Ebola case was announced on October 6. The virus was found in a 40-year-old Kenyan man living in Congo, who travelled to Kenya via Uganda, arriving on October 3.

He tested positive for the disease on October 5 and died on the same day.

Of some 135 who were identified as contacts with the patient, 118 were placed in quarantine, with eight testing positive. They included four health workers and four close family members.

The remaining seven cases are all within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry added.

Nigeria's 1st Ebola case resembles the Kenyan strand

Meanwhile, genomic tests announced by Nigeria's Health Minister have revealed that the Ebola virus found in Kenya's patient zero resembles that found in Nigeria's first case, which was announced earlier this week.

Nigerian health officials detected the infection in the wife of a staff member at Switzerland's embassy in Abuja. She had returned from Uganda on October 3.

On Friday, the Swiss Foreign Ministry denied Ugandan government reports saying the patient had visited the Democratic Republic of Congo, the epicenter of a major Ebola outbreak.

African health authorities are trying to trace the source of the infection. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention had suggested she may have come into contact with Kenya's first patient at the airport. The two flew from Uganda on the same day.

Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said "the viruses are appearing to be related," and the case "is highly similar to that from Kenya."

The current outbreak flared in the DRC in May, and has since spread to Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.

The deadly Bundibugyo species has no approved vaccine or specific treatment.

To date, infections have surpassed 9,700 confirmed cases, including 4,690 deaths, as per World Health Organization figures as of October 20.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Trump eases Canada tariffs ahead of US midterms
entries.summary: The move comes as Trump's Republican Party scrambles to maintain control of the US Congress, with a Republican candidate in a key Senate race saying she had lobbied to lift the tariffs on Canadian products.
entries.content:
October 23, 2026

The move comes as Trump's Republican Party scrambles to maintain control of the US Congress, with a Republican candidate in a key Senate race saying she had lobbied to lift the tariffs on Canadian products.

US President Donald Trump has lifted some of the tariffs imposed on Canada amid an economic row with the US' neighbor to the north, which peaked this summer.

The White House on Friday said the easing of tariffs will apply to products including "plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment."

The changes will take effect on October 30.

While the latest move cuts some of the tariffs, it also imposes new levies on goods including carpets, certain valves and waste products, the White House said.

What do we know about the Canada tariffs relief?

The White House said the president was seeking to offset "the burden to US commerce while better serving the public interest.''

The move comes less than two weeks ahead of the November midterm elections, where Republican candidate Susan Collins is locked in a tight race with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson in Maine.

Collins said on Friday she had addressed the tariffs with Trump's top trade negotiator, Jamieson Greer, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. The senator said she was acting out of concern for "the toll tariffs are taking on Maine families, businesses, farmers, and growers.''

"Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense," Collins said.

She added that she had asked for tariff relief and vowed to "encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner."

Why did Trump impose tariffs on Canada?

Washington and Ottawa have been locked in a trade dispute since Trump returned to the White House last year.

Trade tensions intensified when talks broke down in August, with Trump announcing a 50% levy on some Canadian goods and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announcing retaliatory tariffs.

On Friday, Trump told reporters that "Canada is working very hard to make a deal with us."

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Russia's attacks on Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, are intensifying. DW asked people on the ground what life is like
entries.summary: Russia's attacks on the Ukrainian capital are hitting harder and more frequently, making 2026 one of the long war's bloodiest years for Kyiv. DW asked people on the ground what life is like.
entries.content:
Ukraine

With repeat attacks, Russia has put Kyiv on war's front line

October 23, 2026

Russia's attacks on the Ukrainian capital are hitting harder and more frequently, making 2026 one of the long war's bloodiest years for Kyiv. DW asked people on the ground what life is like.

Until a few months ago, life was relatively peaceful in Kyiv when compared with the situation near the war's front lines elsewhere in Ukraine. Now, as Russia expands its attacks on the capital, Kyiv has increasingly become a front-line city. 

With too few shelters for the 4 million residents of Kyiv, subway stations double as makeshift dormitories. Starting at about 10 every night, people create sleeping areas with mattresses and small tents. Children snuggle up to adults; pets seek comfort from their owners or find a spot among strangers between the cold walls.

"We're alive," Halyna told DW, holding her 5-year-old son, Roman, close. "We've been lucky once again." Most evenings — even when no air-raid siren has sounded — she takes the boy to the nearest subway station. Her apartment is located in the Lukyanivka district, which Russia has systematically targeted over the war's four years and eight months.

'These sick monsters don't care who they kill'

In September, 14-year-old Daniel Umanskyj was doing homework in his room when a Russian drone struck the apartment building in the central district of Pechersk. A neighbor named Vlad happened to be in the hallway with his daughter at the time of the strike. "We were late that day — and this saved our lives," Vlad said. "Daniel's death is a tragedy." He added: "These sick monsters don't care who they kill." Flowers have been planted in front of the damaged apartment building in memory of Daniel.

Russia also targets places where children gather. In early October, a drone struck a school building  in southwestern Kyiv. Fortunately, pupils and teachers were already in shelters at the time.

"We've been teaching all the pupils in person because we have a large shelter that can accommodate more than 500 students," Valentyna Chorna, the school's principal, told DW. As there is enough space in the shelter for everyone, students in the first through ninth grades are able to go to school, she said.

Danger at home, at school — everywhere

Whether classes take place depends not only on the decision of the parents and the school administration: It also depends on whether shelters are available and how long the air-raid siren continues to sound. If an alarm sounds in the morning while children are still at home, they may not be able to go to school that day.

"This is an enormous burden for parents," said a colleague from the DW bureau in Kyiv, whose daughter attends school. "You have to go to work — and the child stays home alone."

"Even the walk to school is dangerous because an air-raid alarm can go off at any time," she said. Her daughter attends a school not far from the Antonov aircraft factory. "One day she texted me: ‘You can't imagine what a huge explosion that was!'" she said. "I don't know if something was shot down or if there was a strike somewhere." She added: "Things like that really scare children." And staying home brings its own risks.

In September, a Russian drone struck their building. The apartment itself wasn't damaged, and her daughter was at school that morning, but it was another reminder of just how much survival has become a matter of luck. When an air-raid siren sounds, no one knows who will be spared, she said.

Kyiv's population persists

Russia's attacks have become deadlier in 2026. According to the military administration in Kyiv, 140 people were killed in the capital during the first eight months of the year, compared with 172 for all of 2025. If this trend continues, 2026 could become Kyiv's deadliest year since the start of the Russian invasion in 2022.

Attacks on warehouses have led to shortages in supermarkets on a scale not seen since the early months of the war. At the end of September, emergency power outages resumed in Kyiv. The subway was paralyzed by a Russian attack. Given the strikes on the energy infrastructure, it is unclear how the capital can reliably supply residents with heat, electricity and water during the upcoming winter.

Despite Russia's attempts to render Kyiv uninhabitable, 72% of the city's residents said in September that they are prepared to endure the war for as long as necessary, the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology reported in early October. The authorities are striving to maintain normal life in the city, where the curfew has been shortened and now runs from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m.

Some facilities have even been allowed to continue operating during "yellow" alerts. During "red" alerts, however, people must immediately seek shelter: This could mean ballistic missiles, cruise missiles or massive combined attacks.

This article was originally written in Ukrainian.
